newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia bonds eye retail data before the big one.
newsitem.headline: Australia bonds eye retail data before the big one.

text.p: *Australian bonds continued to make a steady recovery from the sharp U.S.-led mark down at the start of the week, but the market remains wary of the reaction to Friday's U.S. jobs data.
*Local February retail trade, building approvals due Friday.

Australian bond prices continued to make a steady recovery from the sharp U.S.-led mark down at the start of the week, but the market remains wary of the reaction to Friday's major data for U.S. non-farm payrolls.

Friday also sees the release of local retail trade and building approvals for February, which could also cause the market concern if they show any sign of sustained strength, particularly in the former, analysts said.
Domestic yields eased slightly on Thursday as futures broke resistance at 91.800 on the June 10-year bond contract and 92.70 on the three-year bond.

The market tooks its initial lead from further stability in U.S. Treasuries on Wednesday, but the turnover remained light knowing that a strong U.S. jobs report could fire-up fears of a further tightening by the Federal Reserve in May.

Today's release of Australian February balance of goods and services and February quarter job vacancies failed to make an impression on the market, but both pointed to a continued pick-up in the economy.
The trade balance showed a A$335 million surplus from a revised deficit of A$38 million in January, while vacancies fell 0.9 percent.
Michael Blythe, senior economist at Commonwealth Bank of Australia, said the data suggested that the economy may be picking up more quickly than generally believed.

"While this indicates that the economy is probably not in need of any further monetary policy stimulus, any expectation that the monetary brakes need to be applied any time soon appears misplaced," Blythe said.
"The inflation outlook remains benign and any adjustment to monetary policy appears unlikely over the balance of 1997," he added.

The market showed a strong outperformance against New Zealand, which came under pressure from U.S. selling, putting the N.Z. long-end yields at a premium over Australia for the first time since mid-February. Local spreads also narrowed against the U.S. ahead of today's weekly jobless claims data.
The decisive break of 91.800 on the 10-year bond contract now sees a further barrier at 91.850 before the market can test a one month declining channel at 91.920.
